title: SOAR
summary: Security Orchestration, Automation and Response is the discipline and tooling category concerned with turning detection output into repeatable action. Where a SIEM answers what happened, a SOAR platform asks what should happen next and then does as much of it as is safe without a human. Three capabilities are usually bundled: orchestration, meaning integration with other systems through APIs and playbooks; automation, meaning execution of those playbooks with minimal analyst input; and response, meaning the enrichment, containment and case-management actions that result. Typical first automations are unglamorous and high value: enriching an alert with asset ownership, user directory data, threat-intelligence reputation and recent sign-in history; de-duplicating and grouping related alerts into one case; notifying the right on-call queue with a consistent summary; and posting a structured timeline into the ticketing system. The hard part is not the integration, it is the decision boundary. Automations that take destructive action such as disabling an account, isolating a host or blocking an indicator can cause outages and can be abused by an adversary who learns what triggers them, so mature teams stage actions by confidence and reversibility, require approval for anything irreversible, and log every automated decision with its inputs for later review. SOAR also institutionalises response quality: a playbook is a documented, versioned procedure, so junior analysts execute the same steps as seniors, and post-incident review can show exactly which step failed. Common pitfalls include automating a process nobody had defined, brittle integrations with no error handling, and relying on threat-intelligence indicators that expire before the playbook runs.
objectives: You will be able to distinguish orchestration, automation and response capabilities and map each to concrete SOC workflows.
You will be able to design a playbook that enriches an alert before any containment action is considered.
You will be able to classify response actions by reversibility and confidence, and place approval gates where an automated mistake would cause outage or data loss.
You will be able to write idempotent automation steps so that a retried playbook does not duplicate tickets, notifications or containment actions.
You will be able to instrument playbooks with logging that records inputs, decisions and outcomes for after-action review.
You will be able to evaluate a SOAR integration for failure handling, rate limits, credential storage and blast radius before enabling it.

sources.label: NIST SP 800-61, Computer Security Incident Handling Guide
CISA Cyber Security Incident and Vulnerability Response Playbooks

beginner.definition: SOAR stands for Security Orchestration, Automation and Response. It is a platform that connects your security tools together and runs repeatable response steps for you. Orchestration means the tools talk to each other. Automation means the steps run without a person. Response means real actions, such as blocking or collecting evidence.
beginner.whyItMatters: Analysts waste hours copying data between tools: looking up who owns a machine, checking a user's history, opening a ticket. SOAR does that boring work automatically. This gives analysts time to think. But automation can also cause harm, so risky actions still need a human approval step.
howItWorks: An alert arrives from your detection system and lands in the SOAR queue.
The platform automatically gathers facts: who owns the machine, and how important it is.
It checks threat intelligence to see whether the address or file is already known as bad.
It groups alerts about the same event into one case, so the queue stays clean.
For low-risk steps it acts alone, such as sending a summary to the right team.
For risky steps it pauses and asks a human to approve before anything changes.
beginner.example: Think of a busy airport check-in desk. The clerk does not phone the airline to confirm every booking. The computer already knows the passenger, the seat and the baggage rules. It only calls a supervisor when something unusual appears, like an expired passport. SOAR is that check-in system. It handles the routine questions automatically and pulls in a person only when the decision is risky.
takeaways: Automate the boring, repeatable steps first, and keep risky actions behind approval.
Every automated action should be logged with the inputs that caused it.
Do not automate a process that nobody has written down yet.

exercises.title: SOAR - EASY
exercises.summary: Recall and recognition: definitions, one clear answer, single-step questions.

exercises.title: SOAR - MEDIUM
exercises.summary: Application: read a short log or alert and choose the correct next step.

exercises.title: SOAR - HARD
exercises.summary: Analysis: a multi-step scenario with distractors, evidence to weigh, and a reason to give.

exercises.title: SOAR - EXTREMELY HARD
exercises.summary: Synthesis under pressure: incomplete evidence, competing priorities, and a decision you must defend.
